simples.p.1.text: No signs of manual fraud capable of changing the result were found.

simples.p.2.text: We analyzed the — tally reports from the runoff (the result each voting machine prints at the end of voting) with tests published in scientific journals and already used in elections in Sweden, Senegal, Nigeria and Russia to uncover made-up numbers or “padded” voting machines (references at the end of the page). In almost all of them, 2026 behaves like a normal election, just like 2022. The main exception is voting machines where almost everyone voted, and almost all for Lula: they became more common than in 2022, and this data does not explain why. But there are too few of them to change the result (question 4). Independently of these tests, the OAS electoral observation mission, which followed voting at 977 sections, said it “has no doubts regarding the integrity of the official data” (OAS; question 7).

como-checamos.h2.1.text: How the data was checked, in 1 minute

como-checamos.p.1.text: People are terrible at making up numbers that look random: in experiments, even people paid to draw digits at random use some more than others (Beber and Scacco, 2012). Whoever alters results by hand leaves traces without noticing: digits repeated too often, percentages that are too round (Kobak, Shpilkin and Pshenichnikov, 2016), voting machines with almost everyone voting for the same candidate (Klimek et al., 2012). We looked for these traces in the official data of the TSE (Superior Electoral Court), machine by machine.

como-checamos.p.2.text: To know what is “normal”, we used two yardsticks: what pure chance produces, and the 2022 election, with the same type of voting machine, the same TSE files and exactly the same method. If 2026 stays within both yardsticks, there is nothing out of the ordinary.

numeros-inventados.h3.1.text: Do the numbers look made up?

numeros-inventados.p.1.text: Look at the last digit of each vote count: 1,234 ends in 4; 870 ends in 0. In real votes, this last digit is like a lottery draw: each number from 0 to 9 shows up in roughly 1 out of every 10 voting machines. People who make up numbers tend to use some digits more than others (Beber and Scacco, 2012), and that would show up as taller bars.

numeros-inventados.p.2.text: Result: in 2026, each digit appears at the end of — to — of the counts, for both candidates (we counted the voting machines where the candidate got 10 votes or more). That is exactly what a lottery draw would give.

resultados-redondos.h3.1.text: Are there voting machines with results that are too “round”?

resultados-redondos.p.1.text: If someone adjusted results by hand, there would be too many voting machines with neat percentages, like Lula with exactly 50%, 60% or 70% of the votes: that is what was seen in elections in Russia (Kobak, Shpilkin and Pshenichnikov, 2016). Some voting machines always land on round numbers by pure arithmetic (in a small machine, 100 votes split 50 to 50 give exactly 50%), so the result was compared with what chance produces on its own.

resultados-redondos.p.2.text: In the runoff there are only two candidates, so when Lula has a round percentage, Flávio does too (50% and 50%, 60% and 40%). The test covers both at the same time.

resultados-redondos.p.3.text: Result: — voting machines gave Lula an exact whole-number percentage. Chance alone would give about —. Practically the same number.

urnas-que-destoam.h3.1.text: Does any voting machine stand out too much from its neighbors?

urnas-que-destoam.p.1.text: A single school usually has several voting machines, with voters from the same neighborhood; that is why their results tend to be similar: in the data, the typical difference between a machine and its neighbors is only — times what pure chance would give. A tampered machine would look very different from its neighbors. Even so, some machines stand out naturally: in 2022, — were far above their neighbors and — far below, when a normal curve with the same spread as the data (not pure chance, which would give far fewer) would give about — on each side. That is why what matters is the comparison with 2022. Below, how many voting machines were very different from their neighbors, on each side:

urnas-que-destoam.p.2.text: Result: the numbers are practically the same as in 2022, on both sides, a tiny fraction of the almost 500 thousand voting machines. And — of those that stood out in Lula's favor in the runoff were already above their neighbors in the first round, by a slightly looser yardstick (in 2022, —): these are places that already voted differently, not machines that suddenly changed.

urnas-quase-unanimes.h3.1.text: What about the voting machines where almost everyone voted for the same candidate?

urnas-quase-unanimes.p.1.text: A voting machine where almost everyone voted, and almost all for the same candidate, is the classic sign of a “padded” machine: that is how ballot stuffing was measured in elections in Russia (Klimek et al., 2012). So we counted the runoff voting machines with 95% or more turnout and 90% or more of the votes for a single candidate.

virada-na-apuracao.h3.1.text: Is the turnaround during the count suspicious?

virada-na-apuracao.p.1.text: On election night, the lead changed hands twice. Lula opened the count in front; at 7:45 pm, with 13% of the voting machines counted, Flávio took the lead; at 8:25 pm, with 47%, Lula went back in front and did not lose the lead again (Terra). Tally reports do not arrive in random order: each place finishes voting and transmission at its own time, and the ones that arrived last voted more for Lula. 2022 was similar: Bolsonaro led at the start and Lula pulled ahead with about two thirds of the votes counted (chart below).

virada-na-apuracao.p.2.text: In 2026 there was one more detail. Near the end of voting, Justice Cristiano Zanin, of the STF, extended voting until 7 pm at every section in the country, because of a lack of buses in cities in Bahia: the request reached the STF at 4:32 pm (OAS), and the ruling came out around 5 pm (Gazeta do Povo). Sections that had already closed did not reopen, and in the Federal District the extension was not applied in the end (Rádio Senado). The count started at 5 pm, but the TSE paused it and only resumed it at 7:05 pm, with 1.51% of the votes counted (OAS); — of the votes reached the TSE after 7 pm. In the logs of — randomly drawn voting machines, half had closed by —: the arrival time shows when the tally report was received by the TSE, not when the machine closed (question 8).

virada-na-apuracao.p.3.text: Each line shows one candidate's percentage of the two as the votes were counted. The bottom axis is how much of the count had already been done.

virada-na-apuracao.p.4.text: Result: in both elections, Lula ends up better than he was midway through the count, for the same reason. And, comparing voting machines in the same electoral zone, the ones that arrived late barely differ from the ones that arrived early: the turnaround comes from which places finish counting last, not from the time the votes arrived.

soma-oficial.h3.1.text: Does the sum of the voting machines match the official result?

soma-oficial.p.1.text: The tally reports were added up machine by machine and compared with the totals the TSE publishes by municipality and electoral zone, across the — first-round units. Eligible voters, turnout, abstentions, blank and spoiled votes matched exactly in all of them.

soma-oficial.p.2.text: Valid votes differ in — units, and in each of them the difference is exactly the number of votes cast for Leonardo Alves de Araújo (Leonardo Avalanche, of the PRTB, number 28), — in total. He withdrew his presidential candidacy on September 30, four days before the first round (CNN Brasil), when his number was already on the voting machine. In the per-machine files, these votes appear as votes for him; in the official total, the TSE counts them as “technical spoiled votes”, and the official first-round report shows exactly that number (TSE). None of this has anything to do with the race between Lula and Flávio.

soma-oficial.p.3.text: The runoff totals by municipality and zone were published by the TSE on October 27. In the — units, the sum of the voting machines matched exactly in every field: eligible voters, turnout, abstentions, blank votes, spoiled votes and each candidate's votes, — for Lula and — for Flávio. The same numbers were also checked against the official runoff tallying report (TSE), for the country total and for each of the 27 states and Abroad, with no difference at all.

soma-oficial.p.4.text: What this check shows, and what it does not show: the totals by municipality come from the same count of the tally reports, so it confirms that the TSE's files agree with each other, not that each tally report correctly recorded the votes of its voting machine. Each machine's printed tally report, which is public, checks that the published file is what the machine printed; whether the machine counted correctly is checked by the integrity test and the TSE's audits. In 2022, the Armed Forces' inspection, sent to the TSE by the Ministry of Defense, compared tally reports with the TSE's numbers and found no discrepancy (Jovem Pan); the ministry noted that the work also did not rule out the possibility of fraud, citing, among other points, restrictions on the technicians' access to the voting machines' source code (Ministério da Defesa).

soma-oficial.p.5.text: Result: in both rounds, the sum of the voting machines reproduces the official totals. The only difference, in the first round, is the votes for a candidate who withdrew, counted as spoiled.

alegacoes.h3.1.text: What about the fraud claims made after the runoff?

alegacoes.p.1.text: On the night of the runoff, Flávio Bolsonaro said he did not recognize the election and would ask the TSE to annul it, citing the extension of voting and what he said was the removal of PL inspectors from the secure room (InfoMoney, Gazeta do Povo). The next day, the PL, Flávio's party, released a statement saying it recognizes “the presidential result, proclaimed by the Superior Electoral Court”, but that the questions raised need to be clarified; Flávio then said he would no longer ask for the annulment, and signaled support for a request to revoke the mandate of Lula's ticket (Diário do Nordeste). Eduardo Bolsonaro and Nikolas Ferreira also spoke of fraud, without presenting evidence (Diario de Pernambuco, Estado de Minas). Each argument is below, with what the data shows.

alegacoes.p.2.text: The argument: the eliminated candidates had about 9 million votes and Lula gained more than 10 million, so all of them would have had to go to Lula.

alegacoes.p.3.text: The data: the calculation leaves out two sources of votes. From the first round to the runoff, turnout rose by — and blank and spoiled votes fell by —. Added to the — from all the eliminated candidates, that left — votes for the two finalists. Lula gained — of them (—) and Flávio, —: they did not all need to go to Lula. Because the vote is secret, these numbers are net balances, not each voter's choice (question 6).

alegacoes.p.4.text: The data: the same thing happened in 2022, in the opposite direction. From the first round to the runoff in 2022, Bolsonaro's share of the two candidates rose in — of the — units (the 27 states and Abroad), by between — and —; in 2026, Lula's rose in — of the —, by between — and —. In both elections, whoever grew between the rounds grew across the whole country.

alegacoes.dt.3.text: “The extension until 7 pm changed the rules in the middle of the game”

alegacoes.p.5.text: The facts: Justice Cristiano Zanin, of the STF, extended voting until 7 pm at every section in the country, granting a request from Lula's coalition over the lack of buses in Salvador, Feira de Santana and Lauro de Freitas (Bahia); Flávio's campaign had also asked the TSE for an extension in municipalities in São Paulo, Paraná and Santa Catarina, because of rain (InfoMoney, OAS). The request reached the STF at 4:32 pm, according to the ruling itself (OAS), and the ruling came out around 5 pm (Gazeta do Povo); Exame reported that it applied only to the affected sections, but the ruling covers all of them (OAS). Sections that had already closed did not reopen (Rádio Senado). The OAS observation mission called it unprecedented in Brazilian electoral history, and the TSE's president, Kassio Nunes Marques, said that no rule provided for an extension and that it forced the count's systems to be reorganized (OAS). The claim that PL inspectors were removed from the tallying room was classified as false by the TSE, which says it has videos showing the inspectors' access until the end of the count (Gazeta do Povo).

alegacoes.p.6.text: The data: the voting machines' logs, published by the TSE on the results site, show what time each machine closed and when each vote was recorded. We read the logs of — voting machines drawn at random across the country. In the runoff, half of them had closed by —, and only — of the votes were recorded after 5 pm, Brasília time; in the first round, with no extension, it was —, from voters who were already in line at 5 pm. Only — of the machines stayed open after 6 pm, but the — that stayed open until close to 7 pm received, together, — voters after 5 pm. Projected to the whole country, that would be about — votes after 5 pm (between — and —), — of the final margin: even if all of them went to Lula, the result would be the same.

alegacoes.dt.4.text: “Poll workers voted in place of absent voters” (so-called “voto espírita”, ghost voting)

alegacoes.p.7.text: The facts: the TSE classified the claim as false: voters must show a photo ID, and the identification is recorded (Fast Company Brasil).

alegacoes.p.8.text: The data: there is a related point, shown in question 4: in the voting machines where Lula got 90% or more, more people voted than in 2022, with the same number of registered voters. If poll workers voted in place of absent voters, these machines would have more voters identified without a fingerprint, and votes after 5 pm. The machine logs don't show that. In the logs of — of Lula's — near-unanimous voting machines (for the others, the log doesn't cover the whole vote: one machine was replaced in the middle of the day, and another didn't serve in the first round), — of the runoff votes came from voters identified without a fingerprint, less than in the machines drawn at random across the country (—) and in Flávio's strongholds (—). And manual release by the poll worker, used when the fingerprint of a voter who has fingerprints on file is not recognized, was not concentrated in them: according to the tally reports, which cover every section, it was — of voters in these near-unanimous machines, against — in the other sections of the same polling places; in Lula's strongholds it was — (— at the same polling places), and in Flávio's, — (—). Of the — additional voters from the first round to the runoff in these machines, — were identified by fingerprint, and only — of their votes came after 5 pm. The rise in turnout compared with 2022 remains unexplained in this data, but even if all of the increase above that of the balanced sections, in all sections with 70% or more for Lula, were fake, it would be about — voters, — of the final margin (question 4).

alegacoes.p.9.text: The facts: the last Quaest poll, the day before, had Flávio with 51% and Lula with 49% of the valid votes, a statistical tie within the 2-point margin of error (Exame). Polls miss in both directions: in 2022, the Datafolha poll the day before gave Lula 52% of the valid votes (O Povo), and he finished with —. Polls are not part of this data, and a difference between a poll and the ballot box is not, on its own, a sign of fraud.

alegacoes.p.10.text: Result: the two most repeated calculations, the one about the turnaround and the one about the states, do not hold up against the official numbers. And the logs from a sample of voting machines show that the extension brought in few votes and that Lula's near-unanimous voting machines did not have more voters identified without a fingerprint than the rest of the country.

outros-metodos.h3.1.text: What about other methods, and the voting machines' signatures?

outros-metodos.p.1.text: We applied more tests, from other methods, each built for one type of fraud: a program that acted only on large voting machines, one that switched a fixed percentage of the votes in the runoff, machines standing out from the rest of the polling place, votes added in sections with high turnout, a model that estimates how many sections would have been rigged, and bursts of votes in the machine logs. In the section-size test and in the mixture model, the fraud each one looks for was planted in the real data, and the test found it. In the real data, none showed fraud capable of changing the result. The proportional-switch test cannot decide, but even in the worst case Lula would still win, by about — votes. The test for votes added under high turnout, applied to the whole country, gives an “excess” for Lula because turnout rose more in the states where he is strongest; state by state, the excess is larger for Flávio, as it was for Bolsonaro in 2022. Even counting all of it as fake, Lula would win by —. And the second-digit test “fails” 2022 and 2026 equally: it is not suited to section counts.

outros-metodos.p.2.text: In addition, in — voting machines from the sample, the files' digital signatures were verified: nothing was altered after leaving the machine, the tally report has the published numbers, and the votes in the digital vote record, recounted, match the tally report.

outros-metodos.p.3.text: Result: the other methods reach the same conclusion as the earlier ones, and the files checked are the ones the voting machines signed. The details are in the Technical version, under “More tests”.

com-2018.p.1.text: The 2018 election (Haddad vs. Jair Bolsonaro) was added as a second reference, to see how much the numbers vary from one election to another without fraud. A number that circulated after the runoff: in — sections Lula gained votes and Flávio lost, against — the other way around, a ratio of —. The same calculation gives — in favor of Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 and — in favor of Haddad in 2018, and both of them lost. A model in which nothing abnormal happened, using only each candidate's gain in each municipality, already gives — in 2026: the ratio grows very quickly with the size of the turnaround.

com-2018.p.2.text: We also built a model that predicts each section's runoff without seeing its municipality, and an automatic detector of odd sections. In the model, 2026 falls between 2022 and 2018 or below both, though with more sections deviating in favor of the PT than against it, unlike 2022 and 2018; in the detector, 2026 is close to 2022 (2018 has more sections flagged because it has different levels of blank votes, spoiled votes and section size). Both only catch large or concentrated fraud. The sections the detector finds oddest are, in all three years, those abroad, small ones, those in prisons and those in Indigenous villages.

com-2018.p.3.text: Result: with two reference elections, 2026 does not stand out. The exception is the one in question 4: the near-unanimous sections for the PT (for Lula, —) outnumber those in 2022 and 2018 (—, for Lula, and —, for Haddad). The details are in the Technical version, under “With 2018 too”.

limites.p.1.text: They find numbers made up by hand and “padded” voting machines. They do not find a change that altered every voting machine in the same proportion: all these tests compare each machine with its neighbors, with chance or with 2022, and an equal change in every machine would leave the digits random and each machine similar to its neighbors. For that there are other controls, outside this data: the integrity test and the TSE's audits. Each machine's printed tally report, which is public, does not serve for this, because it comes from the same program; it serves to catch a tally report altered after the voting. In 2026, the OAS observation mission followed the draw and the running of these tests and recommended gradually increasing the sample for the integrity test with biometrics, which is now 10% of the machines drawn (OAS).

tecnico.p.1.text: In — tally reports, neither the round-number tests nor the normal-curve tests show votes made up or added in a quantity capable of changing Lula's runoff victory, by a margin of — votes. The pattern that departs most from 2022, used here as a reference, is sections with near-total turnout and almost all votes for Lula: they became more common, this data doesn't explain why, and, even counting as fake the entire increase in turnout in the sections with 70% or more for Lula above that of the balanced sections, it would be — of the margin.

mais-testes.p.21.text: What it looks for: files altered after leaving the machine, on the way to tallying, which no statistical test catches. Each machine signs with its key the tally report, the digital vote record (RDV, the list of votes, shuffled to keep the ballot secret) and the event log, and the TSE publishes the files and the signatures on the results website. The verification followed the TSE's technical documentation (TSE).

The certificate authorities' keys come from the TSE's technical documentation package, obtained from public copies that match one another, because the TSE website blocks automated downloads; the root certificates are not available for download and were not checked, and the published certificate of the authority that issues those of the oldest machines (2013 and 2015 models) expired in July 2026, although its key verifies the signatures. The program's signature uses a government algorithm with no public specification (CEPESC) and could not be verified. The OAS observation mission recommended increasing the sample for the integrity test with biometrics, now 10% of the machines drawn (OAS).

tres-eleicoes.p.14.text: What it looks for: a change applied to an entire municipality. A model learns, from the sections of other municipalities, how each section's first round (each candidate's votes, blank and spoiled votes, turnout, size, state), plus the change in turnout from the first round to the runoff, predicts its runoff, and then predicts the sections of the municipality it did not see. If an entire municipality had votes switched, it would be far from the prediction. Because it uses the change in turnout, it can absorb added votes that come with higher turnout: what it looks for is switched votes.

tres-eleicoes.p.18.text: What it looks for: sections that are odd in several numbers at once, even if none of them stands out on its own. The Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008) looks at 12 measures of each section in both rounds: each candidate's vote, blank and spoiled votes, turnout, changes between rounds, size and the distance to the rest of the polling place. It was trained on the three elections together, to measure them all with the same yardstick. LOF (Breunig et al., 2000), another method, serves as a second opinion.

In 2018, it is section size in — of those flagged, runoff turnout in — and runoff blank and spoiled votes in —, which in 2018 were at other levels; in 2026, it is first-round turnout, in —, from the sections abroad. Since the detector measures every year with the same yardstick, a year with different typical levels has more sections flagged without being more irregular. The comparison that counts is 2026 with 2022, which have the same reasons and similar rates.

tres-eleicoes.p.22.text: Reading: the detector finds what is unusual, and what is unusual in elections is sections abroad, small ones, in prisons and in indigenous villages, in all three years. It is weak against fraud: moderate stuffing hides among sections that are already unusual by nature. That is why here it complements the tests built for each type of fraud, rather than replacing them.

metodo.li.1.text: Data: TSE open data (dadosabertos.tse.jus.br, resultados-2026, resultados-2022 and resultados-2018), files of votes by section and of details by section (turnout, time the tally report was received, machine model), downloaded on October 26, 2026; to check the runoff, the totals by municipality and zone, each candidate's vote by municipality and zone and the official tallying report, downloaded on October 27; and the runoff tally reports, with the releases by the poll worker in each section, downloaded on October 29. President only.

metodo.li.2.text: Unit: the electoral section, that is, one voting machine and its printed tally report.

metodo.li.3.text: Reference: the 2022 election, with the same type of voting machine and the same file format, processed by the same code; in the “With 2018 too” section, the 2018 election as a second reference, from the same TSE files.

metodo.li.4.text: Tests: last digit (Beber and Scacco, 2012), excess of multiples of 10, spikes at whole percentages (Kobak, Shpilkin and Pshenichnikov, 2016) compared with a resampling of the counts themselves, each section's deviation from its polling place, the turnout × share “fingerprint” (Klimek et al., 2012), atypical changes between rounds, order of arrival of the tally reports, machine model and the sum of the sections against the official totals. In the “More tests” section: section size, proportional migration between rounds, a chi-square by polling place, Shpilkin's method, Benford's second digit (Mebane, 2006), a mixture model (Klimek et al., 2012) and burst votes in the machine logs; in those that look for a type of fraud, it was planted in the real data to measure what the test would see. In the “With 2018 too” section: sections where one candidate gained votes and the other lost, compared with a model with nothing abnormal; vote concentration; a runoff prediction for each section made without seeing its municipality; and an automatic detector (Isolation Forest, Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008, and LOF, Breunig et al., 2000). The full references are at the end of the page.

metodo.li.5.text: Machine logs: — runoff machines read on the TSE results site: all the near-unanimous ones, 250 other Lula strongholds, 150 of Flávio's and 1,000 drawn at random nationwide, with a fixed seed (999, because one was already in another group). In — of them, the number of votes in the log matches the section's official turnout exactly; the other — are machines replaced during voting, whose log only has the votes after the swap. Each machine's time was converted to Brasília time. On the same machines, the digital signatures of the tally report, the RDV and the log were verified and the RDV votes recounted, following the TSE's technical documentation (“More tests” section).

metodo.li.6.text: External check: the national totals summed here are the same as those released by the TSE and reported by the press, in the first round (CartaCapital) and in the runoff (ABC+).

metodo.li.7.text: The vote is secret, so nothing here says how a voter or group of voters voted; all the numbers come from counts by section.

metodo.li.8.text: Limits: these tests catch numbers made up by hand and votes added in individual sections. A change that shifted every machine by the same proportion would leave almost none of these marks (only the swing between rounds would change a little, less than it changes from one election to the next), because the digits would remain random and each machine would remain similar to its neighbors; checking that requires the integrity test and the TSE's machine audits, which are outside this data; the printed tally report does not help, because it comes from the same program.

sim-app.p.1.text: “Yes” means that, looking only at the published numbers, as someone analyzing the election would, the fraud would stand out by the same standard the rest of the page applies to the real numbers: for tests against chance, failing them (last digit, p < 0.001; the others, more than 4 standard deviations); for counts that change from one election to the next, passing 1.5 times the largest value of the reference elections (2022 and, where available, 2018), and by more than chance would explain; for measures whose level changes from one election to the next (the step by section size and the slope of the swing), falling outside the range of the reference elections by more than that range is wide; and, for the Shpilkin method, passing 1.5 times the largest value of the reference elections. “Already stood out without fraud” means the real number already stands out by that standard, so the test can't tell the fraud apart from whatever made the real number high: that is the case of the machines with turnout of 95% or more and 90% or more of the votes for Lula (question 4 of the Summary). The sum of the machines against the official totals isn't on the list: the totals come from the same tally reports, so it matches any fraud done inside the machine.

soma-oficial.p.6.text: In 2026, the OAS electoral observation mission, with 88 observers from 22 countries, visited 977 sections in 21 states, the Federal District and abroad, from the printing of the zero-votes report to the close of voting, and followed the transmission and release of the results, the integrity tests and the check of the voting machines' software. It said that the results released by the TSE are consistent with what its observers saw and that it “has no doubts regarding the integrity of the official data” (OAS). Observers follow the procedures; like these tests, they don't check whether the machine's software counted correctly.

referencias.li.31.text: Organization of American States (OAS). “Preliminary Report of the OAS Electoral Observation Mission in Brazil for the runoff election”, Oct 27, 2026.

data.biometria.desc.text: Voters with fingerprints on file released manually by the poll worker in the 2026 runoff, in every section, from the TSE's tally reports: the total, by group of sections (near-unanimous and strongholds) compared with the rest of their polling place, and the estimate of how these voters voted; and the estimate of voters with no fingerprints on file, from the logs of a sample of voting machines.

alegacoes.p.11.text: How many voted without a fingerprint: according to the tally reports of every section, — voters (— of those who voted) had fingerprints on file and were released manually by the poll worker, from — in — to — in —. Another — or so (—) had no fingerprints on file and were identified by their ID document, as estimated from the logs of — randomly drawn machines; the tally report doesn't count these. How these voters voted is not known: the ballot is secret, and neither the machine log nor the RDV links the way a voter was identified to the vote. What can be measured is something else: among sections at the same polling place, those with more manual releases give Lula slightly more votes. If the voters released by the poll worker alone explained this, they would have given Lula a larger share of the votes between the two candidates than the section's other voters, by — nationally: — in the Northeast, — in the Southeast, — in the North and Center-West, and — in the South, that is, no difference. But fingerprints fail more often with age, so sections with many releases have older voters overall, and the calculation also measures how age relates to the vote in each region; there is no way to tell whether it overstates or understates these voters' difference. Comparing the whole country, without separating polling places, would give —, but that measures the region, not the voters: the Northeast has more manual releases and votes more for Lula.

data.complementos.desc.text: Numbers asked for by the adversarial review of 29/10/2026: sections with atypical turnout that lean to Lula against the share of all sections (and in round 1), the change in turnout from 2022 to 2026 by how strong Lula was in the section, the chi-squared median from chance alone, each voting-machine model against the others where a polling place has several, and Lula's share along the count.

sim-round-row.span.1.text: People who write numbers by hand carelessly tend to end them in 0 or 5; tick it to see what the digit tests catch. A careful forger would write ordinary digits.

fraude.p.2.text: What it's for: it isn't proof of anything about the real election. It's a way to learn by doing: pick a fraud, move the controls and see which tests notice the change and which don't. Each test sees one kind of fraud; none sees them all.
